knowledge_point.title: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to Y

question.:question/problem:
![Directed path C](f00ec157211576e0c3bc299d.png)

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C\left(2 x - 2 y + 1\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $C$ is three quarters of the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{1}=1$, directed counterclockwise from $A=(0,-1)$ to $B=(-3,0)$, as shown above? Do not evaluate the integral.

*Hint: Use the parametrization $\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 \cos{t},\,\sin{t}\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization following the directed path,

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))\,y\prime(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Choose

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 \cos{t},\,\sin{t}\rangle,\qquad \frac{3 \pi}{2}\le t\le 3 \pi.
$$

The squared coordinate ratios sum to $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$, so this parametrization lies on the curve. It travels counterclockwise. The endpoints occur at $t=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ and $t=3 \pi$; the interval covers the specified portion once.

The signed differential factor is

$$
y\prime(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\sin{t}\right)=\cos{t}.
$$

Substituting both coordinates into the given function gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x(t),y(t))&=\left.\left(2 x - 2 y + 1\right)\right|_{x=3 \cos{t},\,y=\sin{t}}\\&=- 2 \sin{t} + 6 \cos{t} + 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, retaining the signed derivative,

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\\&\quad=\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{3 \pi}\left(- 2 \sin{t} + 6 \cos{t} + 1\right)\left(\cos{t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: The upper limit stops before the required traversal is complete.
This expression uses the specified path, substituted function, and signed $y$ derivative.
The coordinates have been interchanged in the substitution into $f$.

question.:question/problem:
![Directed path C](415c30a8753eb94905d3df63.png)

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C\left(x^{2} y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$

where $C$ is three quarters of the circle $\frac{x^2}{1}+\frac{y^2}{1}=1$, directed clockwise from $A=(-1,0)$ to $B=(0,-1)$, as shown above? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization following the directed path,

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))\,y\prime(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Choose

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle \sin{t},\,\cos{t}\rangle,\qquad \frac{3 \pi}{2}\le t\le 3 \pi.
$$

The squared coordinate ratios sum to $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$, so this parametrization lies on the curve. It travels clockwise. The endpoints occur at $t=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ and $t=3 \pi$; the interval covers the specified portion once.

The signed differential factor is

$$
y\prime(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\cos{t}\right)=- \sin{t}.
$$

Substituting both coordinates into the given function gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x(t),y(t))&=\left.\left(x^{2} y\right)\right|_{x=\sin{t},\,y=\cos{t}}\\&=\sin^{2}{t} \cos{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, retaining the signed derivative,

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\\&\quad=-\int_{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}^{3 \pi}\left(\sin^{2}{t} \cos{t}\right)\left(\sin{t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: The upper limit stops before the required traversal is complete.
The squared coordinate was used to the first power.
The coordinates have been interchanged in the substitution into $f$.
The sign of the $y$ coordinate was changed in the substitution.
This expression uses the specified path, substituted function, and signed $y$ derivative.
